meta.description: Not Lord Rochester and not Leonard Lyons. The joke is anonymous, in print by 1946, with a newspaper precursor running in 1916.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Had Six Theories About Bringing Up Children'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to a Restoration earl who died in 1680 and to a 1950s gossip columnist. Quote Investigator traces it to 1946 and calls the creator anonymous.

answer.label: Not Leonard Lyons — the joke is anonymous
answer.authorDates: In print by 1946 · no author has ever been identified
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ finds no substantive link between this joke and any named author. Its earliest close match is a 1946 pamphlet, Parent Education Through Home and School, in which the Rev. James A. Magner quotes it as Lord Rochester’s — but John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester ↗ died in 1680, and QI notes it is “very unlikely that a joke Wilmot wrote or spoke before his death in 1680 was somehow hidden for 266 years and only emerged in 1946”. Leonard Lyons ↗ enters the record only in 1955, when Jacob M. Braude printed a three-children version crediting Lyons and sourcing it to Irving Hoffman of the Hollywood Reporter — nine years after the line was already in print. QI’s verdict: “Currently, the creator is anonymous.”

source.excerpt: “Before I got married,” wrote Lord Rochester, “I had six theories about bringing up children. Now I have six children—and no theories.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ lays out dated citations running from 1904 to 1962 and concludes there is “no substantive support for ascribing the joke to John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester”. Its 1946 pamphlet citation was verified from scans with the help of librarians at Chestnut Hill College, and its November 1946 Oil Weekly citation — where the line is spoken by an unnamed “veteran in the marriage game”, with no Rochester anywhere — was verified from scans too.

Wikipedia’s article on John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester ↗ gives his dates as 1647–1680, an English poet and courtier of Charles II’s Restoration court. That is the arithmetic the attribution has to survive, and does not.

Wikipedia’s article on Leonard Lyons ↗ confirms him as an American newspaper columnist (1906–1976), known for the New York Post column “The Lyons Den”. He was a working columnist in 1955 when Braude’s compilation credited him — but the joke predates that credit by nine years, and Braude’s own entry points at Irving Hoffman, not Lyons.

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for Evan Esar’s The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations ↗ confirms the 1949 edition in which, per QI, Esar printed the joke under the confident heading “ROCHESTER, Lord, 1647-1680, English poet” — lending the attribution a precision it never earned. The volume is lending-restricted, so we did not read the entry ourselves.
source.cutTag: Rev. James A. Magner, Parent Education Through Home and School, 1946
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest close match Quote Investigator has located ↗, and note that the false attribution arrives already attached to it: the pamphlet presents the line as a 266-year-old quotation with no indication of where it found it. A precursor was circulating three decades earlier — a 1916 newspaper filler titled “What She Has”, credited to the Detroit Free Press, which ends with a mother admitting she has “no theories… Just three children.” QI calls the descent of the 1946 quip from that joke “conjectural”, and we do not assert it either.

author.name: Leonard Lyons
author.heading: About Leonard Lyons
author.metaLine: 1906–1976 · American newspaper columnist · "The Lyons Den", New York Post
author.bio: Leonard Lyons was an American newspaper columnist, best known for the New York Post column “The Lyons Den”. Like most gossip columnists of his era he traded in anecdotes and one-liners gathered from around town, which is exactly how a joke with no owner ends up under a byline: in 1955 Jacob M. Braude’s Speaker’s Encyclopedia printed a three-children version of this quip as Lyons’s own reflection after the birth of his third son — while sourcing the item to Irving Hoffman of the Hollywood Reporter. The joke had been in print since 1946.

misattribution.heading: Two men get the credit; neither has a claim
misattribution.intro: A Restoration earl who died in 1680 and a mid-century gossip columnist. The joke belongs to neither.

items.why: The 1946 pamphlet and a June 1947 Reader’s Digest “Quotable Quotes” entry both print it as his. QI ↗ finds no substantive linkage, and the gap is 266 years. It allows that some other Lord Rochester or John Wilmot might have used the line, but has found no evidence of one.

Jacob M. Braude’s 1955 Speaker’s Encyclopedia gives a three-children version as Lyons’s musing after the birth of his third son — and then sources the entry to Irving Hoffman of the Hollywood Reporter. The joke was already in print in 1946 ↗, so 1955 cannot be its origin.

Evan Esar did not just repeat the attribution, he dressed it: QI records ↗ his entry as “ROCHESTER, Lord, 1647-1680, English poet”. Birth and death dates make an attribution look researched, and later compilers copied it forward.

Rev. James A. Magner’s section of Parent Education Through Home and School, quote page 11 — verified by QI from scans ↗. It carries the Rochester credit already, which is why the error is older than every compilation that repeats it.

misattribution.truthLine: No author has ever been identified. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the joke to 1946, finds a 1916 newspaper precursor, and concludes: “Currently, the creator is anonymous.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The thought is older than the joke. In October 1904 the Chicago Daily Tribune reported an address to the Ravenswood Woman’s Club in which Mrs. John McLauchlan told the room that “six children can upset all the theories one ever dared to obtain”, adding that “humility comes with years of motherhood”. QI notes ↗ the resemblance but also that she was not reaching for a laugh.

By January 1916 it had become a gag, syndicated from the Detroit Free Press under the title “What She Has”: a man boasts of his “many splendid theories on the art of bringing up children”, and the woman replies that she has no theories — “just three children.” What 1946 added was compression into a single sentence, the six-and-six symmetry, and a famous dead poet’s name. That is roughly how most quotations acquire their authors.
detailsBody: The variants matter because they show the line being worn smooth by use. November 1946’s Oil Weekly gives it to an unnamed “veteran in the marriage game” with no Rochester at all. A 1949 Kentucky New Era report has a Scout leader telling it about a father of six. Braude’s 1955 compilation drops to three children; so does the columnist Marjorie Mills in January 1962, who introduces it as “that oldie” — sixteen years after its first known printing, it was already folklore.

The pattern is the ordinary life of a joke: it is funny, it is short, and it has no owner, so each retelling attaches whatever name is nearest to hand. The 1946 pamphlet reached for a Restoration rake; 1955 reached for a gossip columnist who had just had a third son. Neither was reporting a source.
context.pull: “Six children can upset all the theories one ever dared to obtain.”

sourcesVerified.claim: QI’s earliest close match is the 1946 pamphlet Parent Education Through Home and School (Rev. James A. Magner, quote page 11, N.C.W.C. Family Life Bureau), which credits “Lord Rochester”; QI finds no substantive linkage to John Wilmot and concludes the creator is anonymous. Braude (1955) credited Leonard Lyons, sourcing it to Irving Hoffman. A 1916 precursor ran as “What She Has”.
John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester, was an English poet and courtier who lived 1647–1680.
Leonard Lyons (1906–1976) was an American newspaper columnist known for the New York Post column “The Lyons Den”.
